Since I usually GM, I don’t have a lot of characters that I played, but I like all of them a lot.

But I’d have to narrow it down to either Tmyan or Hargomme.

Tmyan was an AD&D half-elf Fighter/Magic-user/Thief who liked to push his luck and was willing to sacrifice himself for those he cared about. I played him for years as a kid and eventually turned into an NPC I used in my campaign world who had a lot of misguided attempts at making the world a better place that ran him afoul of the PCs. Due to some magic shenanigans (long story), he was effectively immortal and had been around for thousands of years. When the PCs finally came to “take him down” with a powerful artifact, he welcomed them and accepted it nobly, as he was tired of living.

Hargomme was a character in an Amber campaign that used a variation on Everway (a diceless game system). Likely a child of Eric (for those who know Amber lore), he grew up ignorant of his origins as a servant in a royal household and a soldier, but eventually earned positions as general in the royal mounted forces and and royal spy master before encountering Amberites and being taken away from his home to roam shadow with some others like himself, where they had many adventures and discoveries about both reality and themselves.

My favorite RPG character is myself… give me a long moment, and I shall explain.

When I was about 15 I discovered a game called Mage the Ascension, where you play modern day wizards in a noirish urban fantasy version of Earth, and one of the earliest practice character creation exercises I did was to imagine how my actual life history could have prompted me to join one of the nine factions of wizards in the game (eg if I’d stayed with my intellectual wannabe-science teacher of a father, I’d have wound up as one of the mad scientists who use magic to enforce obsolete pseudoscience theories, while moving in with my neopagan mother instead steered me more toward being one of the sinister super-witches whose power comes from blood rituals and twisted trees). Later in life, as my childish idealism gave way to a more Nietzschean worldview, I also did versions of myself for the game’s “bad guy” factions.

And eventually I decided that all these splinter versions of the same basic personality, who developed different magical practices and powers because of differing life experiences, were all the result of one original wizard, whose life was the same as mine, but who eventually completed the RPG’s “ascend to near-godhood” option. And his version of becoming nigh-omnipotent was to go back through his (my) personal history, figure out every other possible path his life could have taken, and take all of them.

(This rather parallels the way I play SOTM; I’ve always thought that what makes that “Multiverse” in the name is so perfect, is that when you backtrack through a SOTM game that you’ve played, something I used to do a lot when trying to fix errors, even the smallest changes quickly compound on one another, producing a radically different result. You’re told to pick between two heroes that are tied for highest HP to take a bunch of damage, you decide somewhat arbitrarily which one tanks that hit, then a single card play pops out a bunch of minions that all attack the lowest HP, and the one who was tied for highest a minute ago is suddenly KOed. Rewinding and letting the other hero be the one to go down instead can really heavily influence whether the survivor has any hope of pulling off the win.)

Question of the Day #228: Would you want to be cursed with permanent, un-switchable invisibility?

I fully expect that this (along with intangibility) is a likely outcome of IRL death - the classic “ghost” scenario - so I have no particular fear of it, and can very definitely see advantages that I would enjoy exploiting. I think it would be no worse than the condition we’re currently living in, and it might be better, depending on the exact details of how it works (eg probably no hunger, that’s a definite plus, and possibly no fatigue, which would be a minus if it still applied, etc. etc.).

If it’s just invisibility, as with the movie “Hollow Man”, my behavior would probably be similar to that character, albeit a little less openly psychotic (but still fairly predatory, largely out of necessity, since I would no longer have access to the societal mechanisms that enable one to support oneself in a prosocial fashion). I wouldn’t be compelled to act like a Hollywood bad guy, but I would go a little power-mad, partly because I already am mad from lack of power, and partially because of the limited truth behind the extremely overused canard “power corrupts”. It’s not really the power itself which causes the corruption directly; rather, a powerful person tends to become socially isolated, and because we are a species that depends on social bonds to form our sanity, anything which severs us from socialization also erodes our personal foundations.

PS: Ultimately what makes the Hollow Man concept function as a literary trope is the fact that whoever has created the invisibility technology picks some sort of criminal to test it on, because they’re unwilling to kill some loyal soldier by using him as a guinea pig. But by using someone equivalent to what the SCP Foundation calls a “D-class”, you always run the risk that the disposable person you’ve disposed of will not actually go away, and will in fact end up becoming a lot more dangerous to you because of this mistreatment. (The Apotheosis canon segment of the SCP wiki explores this concept in great detail.) The title character in Hollow Man was already a monster even before he gained monstrous power, because of the way that he was rejected by the world around them. Granted, invisibility is a “total villain power” by nature, as Freddy Freeman pointed out, but mind control is often thought of as similarly sinister, and Professor X proves that it doesn’t always have to be. Thusly, if someone along the lines of Captain America had been permanently stuck as the Invisible Thing instead of Sue and Ben, it’s unlikely that Invisi-Steve would go sneaking into women’s bedrooms and having his way with them, as we see HM doing.

(PPS: I honestly thought that the original Invisible Man from the H.G. Wells story was also a criminal like HM, but apparently this confusion comes from either the book or the movie of “League of Extraordinary Gentlemen”, which seemingly pretty much uses HM in place of Wells’s vision of the character. I wish I could track down exactly when I first got these two wildly different stories so thoroughly entangled in my mind, to the point that it’s now nearly impossible for me to separate them.)

Question of the Day #234: What’s one film that you would love to turn into a musical, whether for good or evil?

fjur:

My understanding is that without some sort of heat-protection suit, you wouldn’t last very long.

The flavor text suggests that, but the card mechanics don’t. Nothing deals global fire damage just for being in the area; except for the Behemoths, it seems pretty safe. Very much a case of the Convection Shmonvection trope. As long as you don’t touch the lava, you’re perfectly safe.

As to the Enclave, the heroes get to venture there all the time; humanity only has to die if you become a permanent, immortal resident. As far as we know, Jansa might not care if you just wanted to hang out in a visitor’s lounge for a few decades.

Today’s question: I hate musicals, so no.
